title: Mathematics for Engineers & Scientists
tagline: The mathematical spine of engineering: discrete structures, linear algebra, calculus, probability, and numerical computation.
blurb: Sixteen modules covering the mathematics working engineers and scientists actually use: sets and logic, proof methods, combinatorics, linear algebra through eigenvalues, single- and multi-variable calculus, series, probability, statistics, graphs, and numerical methods. Every module pairs definitions and theorems with worked examples, flashcards, and quick-check quizzes; four Python labs make the math executable (NumPy matrix ops, Monte Carlo estimation, gradient descent, numerical quadrature). Original practice content; confers no certificate.

Count with combinatorics and model discrete structure with graphs and recurrences
Compute with vectors and matrices: products, determinants, inverses, eigenvalues

Reason under uncertainty: probability, Bayes, expectation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests

modules.title: Sets & Propositional Logic
modules.summary: Sets, set operations, propositions, connectives, truth tables, quantifiers, and the logical language every proof in this course is written in.
objectives: Use set notation and the core operations: union, intersection, difference, complement
Evaluate compound propositions with truth tables
Translate statements into quantifier notation
Distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions

notes.title: Sets and operations
notes.body:
A **set** is a collection of distinct objects. `x ∈ A` means x is an element of A. Key operations:
- **Union** `A ∪ B`: everything in A or B
- **Intersection** `A ∩ B`: everything in both
- **Difference** `A \ B`: everything in A but not B
- **Complement** `Aᶜ`: everything in the universe not in A
- **Power set** `P(A)`: the set of all subsets; if `|A| = n`, then `|P(A)| = 2^n`.

notes.title: Propositions and connectives
notes.body:
A **proposition** is a statement that is either true or false, never both. Connectives:
- **Negation** `¬p`: true exactly when p is false
- **Conjunction** `p ∧ q`: true only when both are true
- **Disjunction** `p ∨ q`: true when at least one is true (inclusive or)
- **Implication** `p → q`: false only when p is true and q is false
- **Biconditional** `p ↔ q`: true when p and q agree.
Implication `p → q` is **not** the same as causation — it is a truth-functional claim: 'it is not the case that p holds and q fails.'

notes.title: Quantifiers
notes.body:
**Universal** `∀x P(x)`: P holds for every x. **Existential** `∃x P(x)`: P holds for at least one x.
Negating a quantifier flips it: `¬∀x P(x)` is equivalent to `∃x ¬P(x)`; `∃x ∀y P(x,y)` is generally **not** the same as `∀y ∃x P(x,y)` — order matters. In the definition of a limit, the `∃δ ∀x` ordering is the whole point.

notes.title: Necessary vs sufficient
notes.body: `p → q` says p is **sufficient** for q and q is **necessary** for p. Conflating them is the most common logical error in engineering arguments: 'the tests pass' is not sufficient for 'the code is correct', and 'the code is correct' is not necessary for 'the tests pass.'

cards.front: What is the power set of a set with n elements, and how large is it?
cards.back: P(A) is the set of all subsets of A. |P(A)| = 2^n.
Only when p is true and q is false. All other rows are true.

cards.back: p is sufficient for q; q is necessary for p.

quiz.explain: The existential comes first: a single x that works uniformly for all y — a much stronger claim than ∀y∃x.

quiz.explain: Modus tollens: (build → tests) ∧ ¬tests ⊢ ¬build.

modules.title: Proof Methods
modules.summary: Direct proof, contrapositive, contradiction, and mathematical induction — the four moves that prove theorems, verify algorithms, and certify loop invariants.
objectives: Prove a statement directly from definitions
Use contrapositive and contradiction correctly
Carry out an induction proof including the base case and inductive step
Recognize where induction applies to algorithms and recurrences

notes.title: Direct proof
notes.body: Assume the hypotheses, unpack **definitions**, and derive the conclusion by valid steps. Example: to prove the sum of two even integers is even, write them as `2k` and `2m`; their sum is `2(k+m)`, which is even by definition. Direct proof fails when the definitions give you nothing to grab — then reach for contrapositive or contradiction.

notes.title: Contrapositive and contradiction
notes.body:
**Contrapositive**: prove `¬q → ¬p` instead of `p → q`. Useful when the negated conclusion is easier to work with (e.g., proving '√2 is irrational' style results via parity).
**Contradiction**: assume p and `¬q`, derive a statement that contradicts a known fact or itself. Then `¬q` is impossible, so q holds.

notes.title: Mathematical induction
notes.body:
To prove P(n) for all natural n ≥ n₀:
1. **Base case**: prove P(n₀).
2. **Inductive step**: assume P(k) (the inductive hypothesis) and prove P(k+1).
Then P(n) holds for all n ≥ n₀. Classic: `1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2`. Base n=1: 1 = 1·2/2. Step: adding (k+1) to k(k+1)/2 gives (k+1)(k+2)/2. Strong induction lets the hypothesis assume P(j) for all j ≤ k.

notes.title: Induction in engineering
notes.body: Induction is the proof method for **loop invariants** and **recurrences**: prove the invariant holds before the loop (base), and that each iteration preserves it (step). Recurrence relations like `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n` (mergesort) are solved and verified by the same pattern.

cards.front: The two parts of an induction proof?
cards.back: Base case P(n₀), and the inductive step: P(k) ⇒ P(k+1).

cards.front: Prove p → q by contradiction: what do you assume?
cards.back: Assume p and ¬q together, then derive a contradiction.
n(n+1)/2 — proved by induction.

cards.front: What is a loop invariant, and how is it proved?
cards.back: A property true before and after each loop iteration — proved by induction on the iteration count.
Weak assumes P(k) to prove P(k+1); strong assumes all of P(n₀)...P(k). Strong is needed when P(k+1) depends on earlier cases, e.g. Fibonacci.

quiz.q: In an induction proof of P(n), the inductive hypothesis is:
choices: The assumption P(k) for a fixed k
quiz.explain: We assume P(k) for an arbitrary fixed k and derive P(k+1).

quiz.q: Which proof strategy fits 'If n² is even then n is even'?
choices: Direct from the definition of even

Proof by cases on divisibility by 4
quiz.explain: Direct proof stalls (no handle on n); the contrapositive is easy: odd n = 2k+1 gives n² = 4k²+4k+1, odd.

quiz.q: A proof that assumes the conclusion is guilty of:
quiz.explain: Using the conclusion as a premise is circular — the most common flaw in novice proofs.
Sum of the first n odd numbers is n² — provable by induction.

modules.title: Counting & Combinatorics
modules.summary: Product and sum rules, permutations, combinations, the binomial theorem, and the pigeonhole principle — the mathematics of 'how many'.
objectives: Apply the product and sum rules to counting problems
Distinguish permutations from combinations
Use the binomial theorem and Pascal's identity
Apply the pigeonhole principle

notes.title: Product and sum rules
notes.body: **Product rule**: if a task has k stages with nᵢ, n₂, …, nₖ options, total outcomes = nᵢ·n₂·…·nₖ. **Sum rule**: if two tasks are disjoint, total = sum of their counts. An n-bit string has `2^n` possibilities (product rule); counting them is the same as counting subsets of an n-element set.

notes.title: Permutations vs combinations
notes.body: **Permutation** P(n,k) = n!/(n−k)! — ordered selection of k from n. **Combination** C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!) — unordered selection. Rule of thumb: ask 'does rearranging change the outcome?' If yes, permutation; if no, combination. Choosing a 3-person committee from 10: C(10,3) = 120. Assigning them president/VP/treasurer: P(10,3) = 720.

notes.title: Binomial theorem
notes.body: `(x+y)^n = Σ C(n,k) x^(n−k) y^k` for k=0..n. Pascal's identity `C(n,k) = C(n−1,k−1) + C(n−1,k)` builds the triangle. Setting x=y=1 gives `Σ C(n,k) = 2^n` — the number of subsets of an n-element set, matching the product rule.

notes.title: Pigeonhole principle
notes.body: If n+1 items go into n boxes, some box holds at least 2 items. Generalization: with N items and k boxes, some box holds at least ⌈N/k⌉ items. Used constantly in hashing (collisions are unavoidable when keys exceed slots), scheduling, and lower-bound arguments.

cards.back: n!/(n−k)! — ordered selection.
n!/(k!(n−k)!) — unordered selection.
(x+y)^n = Σ_{k=0}^n C(n,k) x^(n−k) y^k.
n+1 items into n boxes ⇒ some box has ≥2 items.
2^8 = 256 (product rule).
2^n — set x=y=1 in the binomial theorem.

quiz.explain: C(9,4) = 9!/(4!5!) = 126. Order within the team doesn't matter.

choices: Two share a birthday (ignoring leap years)

quiz.explain: 367 people, 366 possible birthdays (incl. Feb 29): some date is shared.

quiz.explain: Each of 6 positions has 26 independent choices: 26^6 (product rule with repetition).

modules.title: Relations & Functions
modules.summary: Injective, surjective, and bijective functions; composition and inverses; equivalence relations and partitions — the language of mappings between structures.
objectives: Classify functions as injective, surjective, or bijective
Compose functions and find inverses
Verify an equivalence relation and describe its classes
Connect bijections to counting (cardinality)

notes.title: Function properties
notes.body: f: A → B is **injective** (one-to-one) if f(x₁)=f(x₂) implies x₁=x₂ — distinct inputs map to distinct outputs. **Surjective** (onto) if every y in B has some x with f(x)=y — the image covers B. **Bijective** if both: a perfect pairing, which is exactly when an **inverse** f⁻¹: B → A exists.

notes.title: Composition
notes.body: (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)): apply f first, then g. Composition is **associative** but generally **not commutative** — order matters. If f and g are both bijective, g∘f is bijective with inverse f⁻¹∘g⁻¹ (note the reversed order).

notes.title: Equivalence relations
notes.body: A relation ~ on A is an **equivalence relation** if it is: **reflexive** (x~x), **symmetric** (x~y ⇒ y~x), **transitive** (x~y, y~z ⇒ x~z). Every equivalence relation **partitions** A into disjoint equivalence classes. Example: congruence mod n partitions the integers into n residue classes — the foundation of modular arithmetic used in cryptography.

notes.title: Partial orders (glimpse)
notes.body: Replace symmetric with **antisymmetric** (x≤y, y≤x ⇒ x=y) and you get a **partial order** — reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive. Task-dependency graphs, version ordering, and type hierarchies are partial orders; topological sort linearizes them.

cards.back: Injective: distinct inputs → distinct outputs. Surjective: image covers the codomain. Bijective: both — invertible.
f⁻¹∘g⁻¹ — order reverses.

cards.front: Three properties of an equivalence relation?
cards.back: Reflexive, symmetric, transitive.
Five classes: [0],[1],[2],[3],[4] — the residue classes.

cards.front: What does a bijection between finite sets tell you?
cards.back: They have the same cardinality — counting via pairing.

quiz.explain: f(0)=f(1)=f(−1)=0, so not injective; as a continuous cubic with limits ±∞ it attains every real value, so surjective.

quiz.q: Which relation on ℤ is an equivalence relation?
quiz.explain: Same parity: reflexive, symmetric, transitive. < is not symmetric; divisibility is not symmetric; x+y>0 fails reflexivity (0+0>0 false).

quiz.q: (g∘f)(x) means:
quiz.explain: Rightmost applies first: (g∘f)(x) = g(f(x)).

quiz.explain: A bijection pairs elements one-to-one, so the sets have equal cardinality.

modules.title: Linear Algebra I — Vectors & Spaces
modules.summary: Vectors, dot products, vector spaces, span, and linear independence — the geometric core behind graphics, ML features, and simulation.
objectives: Add, scale, and take dot products of vectors
Test a set for linear independence
Describe span and identify a basis
Compute projections and angles via the dot product

notes.title: Vectors and the dot product
notes.body: A vector **v** in ℝⁿ is an ordered n-tuple. Addition and scalar multiplication are componentwise. The **dot product** `u·v = Σ uᵢvᵢ` measures alignment: `u·v = |u||v|cos θ`. The **norm** `|v| = √(v·v)`. Two nonzero vectors are **orthogonal** iff their dot product is 0.

notes.title: Vector spaces
notes.body: A **vector space** is a set closed under addition and scalar multiplication, satisfying the vector axioms (associativity, zero vector, additive inverses, distributivity). Examples: ℝⁿ, matrices of fixed size, polynomials of degree ≤ n, functions ℝ → ℝ. Closure is the key test: is the sum of two members always a member?

notes.title: Span and linear independence
notes.body: The **span** of a set is all its linear combinations. Vectors v₁..vₖ are **linearly independent** if `c₁v₁+…+cₖvₖ = 0` forces all cᵢ = 0 — no vector is a combination of the others. A **basis** is an independent spanning set; every vector has a **unique** coordinate representation in a basis. dim(ℝⁿ) = n.

notes.title: Projection
notes.body: The projection of u onto v is `proj_v(u) = ((u·v)/(v·v)) v`. This single formula powers least-squares fitting, Gram–Schmidt orthogonalization, and attention-free similarity search: the dot product with a unit vector is the signed length of the projection.

cards.front: u·v in terms of norms and angle?
cards.back: u·v = |u||v|cos θ.

cards.front: When is a set of vectors linearly independent?
cards.back: When c₁v₁+…+cₖvₖ=0 implies every cᵢ=0.

cards.front: What is a basis? What is dimension?
cards.back: An independent spanning set; the number of vectors in any basis.

cards.front: Maximum size of an independent set in ℝⁿ?
cards.back: n — any n+1 vectors in ℝⁿ are dependent.

cards.front: What is the norm |v| in terms of the dot product?

quiz.explain: c₁(1,2)+c₂(3,4)=(0,0) gives c₁+3c₂=0, 2c₁+4c₂=0 ⇒ only c₁=c₂=0.

Which set is a basis of ℝ³?
quiz.explain: Three vectors in ℝ³ that are independent and span — the standard basis. The others are too few or dependent.

modules.title: Linear Algebra II — Matrices
modules.summary: Matrix multiplication, transposes, determinants, inverses, and rank — the computational engine of applied mathematics.
objectives: Multiply matrices with correct dimensions
Compute 2×2 and 3×3 determinants
Invert a matrix and test invertibility
Find rank and interpret it

notes.title: Matrix multiplication
notes.body: If A is m×n and B is n×p, then AB is m×p with `(AB)ᵢⱼ = Σₖ AᵢₖBₖⱼ` — row i of A dotted with column j of B. The inner dimensions must match. Multiplication is **associative** and distributes over addition, but is **not commutative**: AB ≠ BA in general. `(AB)ᵛ = BᵛAᵛ` — order reverses, like function composition.

notes.title: Determinants
notes.body: The determinant measures signed volume scaling. 2×2: `det [[a,b],[c,d]] = ad − bc`. 3×3: cofactor expansion along any row/column. det(A) ≠ 0 iff A is invertible; det(AB) = det(A)det(B). A zero determinant means the transformation collapses at least one dimension.

notes.title: Inverses
notes.body: A⁻¹ satisfies AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I. 2×2: `[[a,b],[c,d]]⁻¹ = (1/(ad−bc)) [[d,−b],[−c,a]]`. For larger matrices use Gauss–Jordan elimination on [A|I]. `(AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹`. Never compute an explicit inverse to solve Ax=b in practice — factor instead (LU/QR); inversion is slower and less stable.

notes.title: Rank
notes.body: **Rank** = number of linearly independent rows = number of independent columns = dimension of the column space. For Ax=b: rank(A) = rank([A|b]) means a solution exists; rank(A) = n (full column rank) means it is unique. Rank deficiency signals redundancy — or multicollinearity in data.

cards.front: When can you multiply A (m×n) by B?
cards.back: B must be n×p; the result is m×p.
det = ad−bc; inverse = 1/det · [[d,−b],[−c,a]].
(AB)ᵛ = BᵛAᵛ; (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹.
A is not invertible; it collapses dimension (zero volume scaling).
Number of independent rows/columns = dim of column space.

cards.front: Why not solve Ax=b via x = A⁻¹b numerically?
cards.back: Explicit inversion is slower and numerically less stable than factorization (LU/QR).

quiz.explain: Multiplying by the identity leaves A unchanged.

quiz.q: A is 3×2, B is 2×4. Shape of AB?
quiz.explain: Inner dims agree (2); outer dims give 3×4.

quiz.q: If rank(A) = 2 for a 4×3 matrix A, then Ax = 0 has:
quiz.explain: 3 columns but rank 2 ⇒ columns dependent ⇒ nontrivial null space ⇒ infinitely many solutions.

modules.title: Linear Algebra III — Eigenvalues
modules.summary: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, diagonalization, and symmetric matrices — the structure behind PCA, stability analysis, and PageRank.
objectives: Solve det(A − λI) = 0 for eigenvalues
Find eigenvectors for a given eigenvalue
Test whether a matrix is diagonalizable
State the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices

notes.title: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
notes.body: A nonzero vector v is an **eigenvector** of A with **eigenvalue** λ if `Av = λv` — A stretches v without rotating it. Eigenvalues solve the **characteristic equation** `det(A − λI) = 0`. For 2×2 this is a quadratic; its roots are the eigenvalues (possibly complex).

notes.title: Diagonalization
notes.body: A is **diagonalizable** if A = PDP⁻¹ with D diagonal: then Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹, and powers become trivial. A sufficient condition: n distinct eigenvalues for an n×n matrix. Diagonalization is why eigenvalues govern long-term behavior — Markov chains, linear recurrences, and dynamical systems all reduce to 'λᵏ grows or decays?'

notes.title: Symmetric matrices
notes.body: The **spectral theorem**: every real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis. Covariance matrices are symmetric, so PCA's principal components are real, orthogonal directions — no complex arithmetic, no defective cases.

notes.title: Trace and determinant via eigenvalues
notes.body: **Trace**(A) = sum of diagonal entries = sum of eigenvalues. **det**(A) = product of eigenvalues. Quick sanity checks: for [[4,1],[2,3]], trace 7 and det 10, so eigenvalues sum to 7 and multiply to 10 — they are 5 and 2.

cards.back: det(A − λI) = 0; its roots are the eigenvalues.
A = PDP⁻¹ exists when A has n distinct eigenvalues (n×n).
Real symmetric matrices have real eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis.
trace = sum of eigenvalues; det = product of eigenvalues.
If A = PDP⁻¹, then Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹ — powers act diagonally on eigen-components.

quiz.q: Eigenvalues of [[2,0],[0,5]]?
quiz.explain: Diagonal matrix: eigenvalues are the diagonal entries.

quiz.q: Eigenvalues of [[4,1],[2,3]]?
An eigenvector v of A with eigenvalue 3 satisfies:
quiz.explain: Definition: Av = λv with v ≠ 0.

quiz.q: A real symmetric 3×3 matrix must have:
quiz.explain: Spectral theorem: real eigenvalues, orthonormal eigenbasis. Distinctness and det=1 are not guaranteed.

modules.title: Calculus I — Limits & Derivatives
modules.summary: Limits, continuity, the derivative as a rate of change, and the differentiation rules — the mathematics of change.
objectives: Evaluate limits including indeterminate forms
Differentiate using product, quotient, and chain rules
Interpret the derivative as rate of change and slope
Find critical points and classify extrema

notes.title: Limits and continuity
notes.body: `lim(x→a) f(x) = L` means f(x) can be made arbitrarily close to L by taking x close to a. f is **continuous** at a if the limit equals f(a). Indeterminate forms 0/0 or ∞/∞: try factoring, rationalizing, or **l'Hôpital's rule** — differentiate numerator and denominator separately (check the form first!).

notes.title: The derivative
notes.body: `f'(x) = lim(h→0) [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h` — instantaneous rate of change, slope of the tangent line. Rules: **power** `(xⁿ)' = nxⁿ⁻¹`; **product** `(uv)' = u'v + uv'`; **quotient** `(u/v)' = (u'v − uv')/v²`; **chain** `[f(g(x))]' = f'(g(x))·g'(x)`. The chain rule is the workhorse — it is also what backpropagation computes.

notes.title: Key derivatives
notes.body: Memorize: `(eˣ)' = eˣ`; `(ln x)' = 1/x`; `(sin x)' = cos x`; `(cos x)' = −sin x`; `(aˣ)' = aˣ ln a`; `(arctan x)' = 1/(1+x²)`. Every ML loss gradient is built from these plus the chain rule.

notes.title: Optimization
notes.body: **Critical points**: f'(x) = 0 or undefined. **First derivative test**: sign change of f' classifies max/min. **Second derivative test**: f''(c) > 0 ⇒ local min; f''(c) < 0 ⇒ local max at a critical point c. On a closed interval, also check the endpoints — global extrema live at critical points or boundaries.

cards.back: lim(h→0) [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h.

cards.front: Derivatives of eˣ, ln x, sin x, cos x?
cards.back: eˣ; 1/x; cos x; −sin x.
For 0/0 or ∞/∞: lim f/g = lim f'/g' (if the latter exists).
f'(c)=0, f''(c)>0 ⇒ local min; f''(c)<0 ⇒ local max.

cards.back: At a critical point inside, or at an endpoint a or b.

modules.title: Calculus II — Integration
modules.summary: Antiderivatives, the Fundamental Theorem, integration techniques, and improper integrals — accumulation made rigorous.
objectives: State and apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
Integrate by substitution and by parts
Evaluate improper integrals via limits
Compute areas, volumes, and averages with integrals

notes.title: The Fundamental Theorem
notes.body: **FTC Part 1**: if F(x) = ∫[a→x] f(t) dt, then F'(x) = f(x) — differentiation undoes accumulation. **FTC Part 2**: `∫x[a→b] f = F(b) − F(a)` for any antiderivative F. This is why we can evaluate definite integrals by finding antiderivatives instead of Riemann sums.

notes.title: Techniques
notes.body: **Substitution**: `∫ f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du` with u = g(x) — the chain rule in reverse. **Integration by parts**: `∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du` — choose u by LIATE priority (Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential). **Partial fractions** split rational functions into integrable pieces.

notes.title: Improper integrals
notes.body: Integrals over infinite intervals or with singularities are defined by **limits**: `∫[1→∞] (1/x²) dx = lim(b→∞) [1 − 1/b] = 1` — converges. But `∫[1→∞] (1/x) dx` diverges (grows like ln b). Always split at each singularity and take limits separately.

notes.title: Applications
notes.body: Area between curves: `∫ (top − bottom) dx`. Volume of revolution (disks): `π∫ [f(x)]² dx`. **Average value** of f on [a,b]: `(1/(b−a)) ∫[a→b] f`. Expected value in probability is exactly this idea with a density function.

cards.back: ∫[a→b] f = F(b) − F(a) for any antiderivative F.
∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du.
Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential.
No — it diverges like ln b.

modules.summary: Convergence tests, power series, and Taylor expansions — how functions become computable polynomials.
objectives: Test series for convergence with the standard tests

notes.title: Convergence tests
notes.body: **Divergence test**: if aₙ ⇛ 0, Σaₙ diverges. **Integral test**: compare Σf(n) with ∫f. **p-series** Σ1/nᵖ converges iff p > 1. **Ratio test**: L = lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ|; L<1 converges, L>1 diverges, L=1 inconclusive. **Alternating series test**: decreasing terms → 0 implies convergence.

notes.title: Power series
notes.body: `Σ cₙ(x−a)ⁿ` converges on an interval around a. The **ratio test** gives the **radius of convergence** R: converge for |x−a|<R, diverge outside; check endpoints individually. Example: `Σ xⁿ/n!` has R = ∞.

notes.title: Taylor series
notes.body: `f(x) = Σ fⁿ(a)/n! · (x−a)ⁿ`. Maclaurin (a=0) essentials: `eˣ = Σ xⁿ/n!`; `sin x = Σ (−1)ⁿ x^(2n+1)/(2n+1)!`; `cos x = Σ (−1)ⁿ x^(2n)/(2n)!`; `1/(1−x) = Σ xⁿ` for |x|<1; `ln(1+x) = Σ (−1)ⁿ⁺¹ xⁿ/n` for |x|<1, x≠−1.

notes.title: Error bounds
notes.body: **Taylor's inequality**: |Rₙ(x)| ≤ M|x−a|ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)! where M bounds |fⁿ⁺¹|. This is how calculators guarantee digits: pick n so the bound beats your tolerance. Alternating series have an even simpler bound — the error is at most the first dropped term.

modules.summary: Partial derivatives, gradients, the chain rule in higher dimensions, and optimization of functions of several variables.
objectives: Compute partial derivatives and gradients

Find and classify critical points of f(x,y)

notes.title: Partial derivatives and the gradient
notes.body: `∂f/∂x` treats other variables as constants. The **gradient** `∇f = ⟨f_x, f_y, f_z⟩` points in the direction of **steepest increase**; its magnitude is the slope in that direction. The **directional derivative** in unit direction u is `D_u f = ∇f · u`.

notes.title: Chain rule and differentials
notes.body: If z = f(x,y) with x(t), y(t): `dz/dt = f_x dx/dt + f_y dy/dt`. The **total differential** `dz = f_x dx + f_y dy` is the linear approximation — the seed of error propagation: small input errors scale by the partial derivatives.

notes.title: Critical points in 2D
notes.body: Critical point: `∇f = 0` (or undefined). **Second derivative test** with `D = f_xx f_yy − (f_xy)²`: D>0 and f_xx>0 ⇒ min; D>0 and f_xx<0 ⇒ max; D<0 ⇒ **saddle point**; D=0 inconclusive. Saddles are the generic obstacle in neural-network training.

notes.title: Lagrange multipliers
notes.body: To optimize f(x,y) subject to g(x,y)=c, solve `∇f = λ∇g` together with the constraint. Geometrically: at the optimum the level curves are tangent. Example: maximize xy subject to x+y=10 ⇒ ⟨1/y⟩... solving gives x=y=5, value 25.

modules.title: Probability
modules.summary: Axioms, conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, random variables, and expectation — reasoning under uncertainty.
objectives: Apply the probability axioms and counting to probability
Compute conditional probabilities and use Bayes' theorem
Find expectation and variance of a random variable
Work with the binomial and normal distributions

notes.title: Axioms and basic rules
notes.body: **Kolmogorov axioms**: P(A) ≥ 0; P(S) = 1; disjoint events add. Consequences: P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A); **addition rule** P(A∪B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Two events are **independent** iff P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B) — independence is a property of the probability measure, not of intuition.

notes.title: Conditional probability and Bayes
notes.body: `P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B)`. **Law of total probability**: P(B) = Σ P(B|Aᵢ)P(Aᵢ). **Bayes' theorem**: `P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)` — update prior belief P(A) with evidence B. Base-rate neglect (ignoring P(A)) is the classic applied error: a 99%-accurate test on a 1-in-10,000 condition still yields mostly false positives.

notes.title: Random variables, expectation, variance
notes.body: A **random variable** X maps outcomes to numbers. **Expectation** E[X] = Σ xᵢP(X=xᵢ) (discrete) or ∫ x f(x)dx (continuous) — the long-run average. Linearity: E[aX+bY] = aE[X]+bE[Y] even when dependent. **Variance** Var(X) = E[(X−E[X])²] = E[X²]−E[X]²; standard deviation σ = √Var.

notes.title: Binomial and normal
notes.body: **Binomial**(n,p): P(X=k) = C(n,k)pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ; E[X]=np, Var=np(1−p). **Normal** N(μ,σ²): the bell curve; the **68–95–99.7 rule** for ±1,2,3 σ. Standardize with Z = (X−μ)/σ. The normal is the limit of sums — which is the Central Limit Theorem, next module.

cards.back: P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B).

cards.back: P(A∩B) = P(A)P(B).

modules.title: Statistics
modules.summary: Sampling, the Central Limit Theorem, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing — inference from data to populations.
objectives: Explain the Central Limit Theorem and its conditions
Construct and interpret a confidence interval
Run a hypothesis test and interpret the p-value correctly
Distinguish correlation from causation

notes.title: Sampling and the CLT
notes.body: A **statistic** (e.g., sample mean x̄) estimates a **parameter** (μ). The **Central Limit Theorem**: for iid samples with mean μ and finite variance σ², x̄ is approximately N(μ, σ²/n) for large n — regardless of the population's shape. Standard error of the mean = σ/√n. This is why averages of enough data behave normally.

notes.title: Confidence intervals
notes.body: A 95% CI for μ: `x̄ ± z*·σ/√n` (z* ≈ 1.96; use t* for small n or estimated σ). Correct interpretation: **95% of intervals constructed this way capture the true μ** — not 'there is a 95% chance μ is in this interval.' Width shrinks as 1/√n: quadrupling the sample halves the width.

notes.title: Hypothesis testing
notes.body: H₀ (null) vs H₁ (alternative). The **p-value** = P(data this extreme | H₀ true) — **not** P(H₀ true | data). Reject H₀ if p < α (often 0.05). **Type I error**: rejecting a true H₀ (rate α). **Type II error**: missing a real effect; **power** = 1 − P(Type II). Practical significance ≠ statistical significance.

notes.title: Correlation is not causation
notes.body: Correlation measures linear association (−1 ≤ r ≤ 1). Confounders, reverse causation, and selection effects produce correlations without causation. The honest pipeline: randomize (experiments), control (regression), or instrument — and report effect sizes with uncertainty, not just p-values.

cards.back: Sample means of iid data with finite variance are approx. normal: x̄ ~ N(μ, σ²/n) for large n.
95% of such intervals capture the true parameter — a property of the procedure, not of this interval.
P(data at least this extreme | H₀ true). Not P(H₀ is true).

cards.front: Type I vs Type II error?
cards.back: Type I: false positive (reject true H₀). Type II: false negative (miss a real effect).

cards.front: How does CI width scale with sample size?
cards.back: Proportional to 1/√n — 4× data halves the width.

choices: 95% of intervals from this procedure contain μ
quiz.explain: Frequentist CIs describe the procedure's long-run capture rate, not a probability about this fixed interval.

quiz.q: p = 0.03 with α = 0.05. Decision?
quiz.explain: p < α ⇒ reject the null at the 5% level.

quiz.q: Standard error of the mean for σ=10, n=100?

quiz.explain: Correlation alone never establishes causation — confounders and reverse causation remain open.

modules.title: Graphs & Recurrences
modules.summary: Graph terminology, trees, traversal orders, and solving recurrence relations — the discrete structures behind networks and algorithms.
objectives: Use graph vocabulary: degree, path, cycle, connectivity
Characterize trees and count their edges
Trace BFS and DFS orders
Solve linear recurrences (Fibonacci, divide-and-conquer)

notes.title: Graph basics
notes.body: A **graph** G=(V,E): vertices and edges. **Degree** of v = incident edges. **Handshaking lemma**: Σ deg(v) = 2|E| — every edge contributes 2. A **path** with no repeated vertices; a **cycle** returns to start. **Connected** = a path exists between every pair. A **complete graph** Kₙ has n(n−1)/2 edges.

notes.title: Trees
notes.body: A **tree** is a connected acyclic graph. Equivalent characterizations: connected with n−1 edges; acyclic with n−1 edges; exactly one simple path between any two vertices. A **spanning tree** of G is a tree on all of G's vertices — minimum spanning trees (Kruskal/Prim) minimize total edge weight.

notes.title: BFS and DFS
notes.body: **BFS** (queue): explores level by level — finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. **DFS** (stack/recursion): goes deep first — detects cycles, produces topological orderings. Both visit each vertex and edge once: O(V+E). Choose BFS for shortest-path, DFS for structure (components, cycles, topo sort).

notes.title: Recurrence relations
notes.body: Define sequences by earlier terms: Fibonacci `Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂`, F₀=0, F₁=1. **Linear recurrences** with constant coefficients solve via the **characteristic equation**: for aₙ = c₁aₙ₋₁ + c₂aₙ₋₂, solve r² = c₁r + c₂. Divide-and-conquer recurrences like T(n) = 2T(n/2)+n solve to Θ(n log n) — the Master Theorem generalizes this.

cards.back: Σ deg(v) = 2|E|.

cards.front: Three equivalent definitions of a tree?
cards.back: Connected + acyclic; connected with n−1 edges; unique simple path between any two vertices.

cards.front: BFS vs DFS: data structure and use?
cards.back: BFS: queue, shortest paths unweighted. DFS: stack/recursion, cycles and topological order.
Fₙ=Fₙ₋₁+Fₙ₋₂, F₀=0, F₁=1.
Θ(n log n) — mergesort's recurrence.

modules.title: Numerical Methods
modules.summary: Bisection, Newton's method, numerical integration, and error analysis — computing answers when closed forms don't exist.
objectives: Bracket a root with bisection and bound its error
Apply Newton's method and state its convergence requirement
Approximate integrals with trapezoidal and Simpson's rules
Quantify error order and condition sensitivity

notes.title: Bisection
notes.body: If f is continuous with f(a)f(b) < 0, a root lies in (a,b). Halve repeatedly, keeping the sign change: after n steps the error is at most (b−a)/2ⁿ. **Guaranteed but linear** convergence — slow and sure. Always check the sign-change precondition; without it, bisection proves nothing.

notes.title: Newton's method
notes.body: `xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ)/f'(xₙ)` — follow the tangent line to its x-intercept. Near a simple root it converges **quadratically** (correct digits roughly double per step). Requirements: a good starting guess, f'(xₙ) ≠ 0, and smoothness. Bad starts diverge or cycle — pair with bisection bracketing for safety.

notes.title: Numerical integration
notes.body: **Trapezoidal rule**: h/2 · [f₀ + 2f₁ + … + 2fₙ₋₁ + fₙ], error O(h²). **Simpson's rule** (n even): h/3 · [f₀ + 4f₁ + 2f₂ + … + 4fₙ₋₁ + fₙ], error O(h⁴) — halving h cuts Simpson error ~16×. Simpson fits parabolas; it is exact for cubics too.

notes.title: Error and conditioning
notes.body: Two error sources: **truncation** (method's approximation) and **roundoff** (finite precision). **Conditioning** measures sensitivity: solving near-singular systems amplifies input errors — the condition number κ(A) = ||A||·||A⁻¹|| bounds the blowup. A stable algorithm on an ill-conditioned problem still gives garbage: distinguish the two.

cards.back: xₙ₊₁ = xₙ − f(xₙ)/f'(xₙ).
h/3 · [1, 4, 2, 4, 2, …, 4, 1]; n must be even; error O(h⁴).
Truncation: error from the method's approximation. Roundoff: error from finite floating-point precision.

cards.front: What does the condition number measure?
cards.back: Sensitivity of the problem's answer to input perturbations — not the algorithm's quality.

quiz.explain: Division by f'(xₙ): a zero derivative blows up the step (also bad for flat regions and poor starts).

modules.title: Linear Systems & Optimization
modules.summary: Gaussian elimination, LU factorization, least squares, and gradient descent — solving systems and minimizing objectives at scale.
objectives: Solve Ax=b by Gaussian elimination with back substitution
Formulate and solve a least-squares problem
Run gradient descent on a convex objective
Explain the normal equations and when to avoid them

notes.title: Gaussian elimination
notes.body: Forward elimination reduces [A|b] to upper-triangular form using row operations (swap, scale, add multiples); **back substitution** solves from the bottom up. Cost: O(n³). **Partial pivoting** (swap in the largest available pivot) controls roundoff — never divide by a tiny pivot when a larger one is available.

notes.title: LU factorization
notes.body: Elimination factors A = LU (lower × upper, with row permutations). Factor once at O(n³), then solve each new right-hand side at O(n²) via Ly=b, Ux=y. This is what libraries actually do — `numpy.linalg.solve` uses LU-style factorization, not explicit inversion.

notes.title: Least squares
notes.body: For overdetermined Ax ≈ b, minimize ||Ax−b||². Setting the gradient to zero gives the **normal equations** `AᵛAx = Aᵛb`. Geometrically: project b onto the column space of A. In practice prefer **QR factorization** — the normal equations square the condition number (κ(AᵛA) = κ(A)²), amplifying numerical error.

notes.title: Gradient descent
notes.body: `x ← x − α∇f(x)`: step downhill. For convex f with Lipschitz gradient, a small enough **learning rate** α converges; too large diverges. **Stochastic** GD uses one sample's gradient per step — noisy but fast per iteration, the engine of neural-network training. The gradient itself comes from the chain rule (module 8).

cards.back: O(n³) for the factorization; O(n²) per solve after LU.
AᵛAx = Aᵛb — least-squares solution of Ax≈b.

cards.back: Normal equations square the condition number: κ(AᵛA)=κ(A)².

scenarios.title: Choosing a Root-Finding Method
scenarios.context: You must find where a sensor calibration curve f(x) crosses zero on [0, 5]. f is smooth, you can evaluate f and f' cheaply, and you know f(0) < 0 < f(5). A wrong answer ships bad calibrations.

steps.prompt: First decision: which method do you start with?

options.text: Bisection on [0,5] — guaranteed, then polish with Newton
options.why: The sign change guarantees a root exists; bisection brackets it safely, and Newton's method then converges quadratically near the root.
Newton's method has no global guarantee — a poor start can diverge or cycle. Bracket first.

options.text: Sample f at 1000 points and pick the smallest |f|
options.why: Grid sampling gives no error bound and can miss narrow crossings entirely.

steps.prompt: After bisection narrows the bracket to width 1e-3, the root is needed to 1e-9. Next step?

options.text: Switch to Newton's method inside the bracket
options.why: Quadratic convergence near a simple root reaches 1e-9 in a few iterations from a 1e-3 bracket.
Works but wasteful: bisection needs ~10 more steps per decimal digit; Newton does it in 2-3.
The requirement is 1e-9; shipping 1e-3 violates the spec.

scenarios.title: Which Statistical Test?
scenarios.context: Two web-page variants ran for a week: A converted 120/2000 visitors, B converted 150/2000. The team wants to know if B is really better or the gap is noise.

steps.prompt: What is the right first analysis?

options.text: Two-proportion z-test (or chi-square) for the difference
options.why: Two independent binomial proportions — the z-test for difference in proportions (equivalently chi-square) is the standard tool.

options.text: A t-test on the raw conversion counts
options.why: A t-test assumes roughly normal continuous data; these are binary outcomes aggregated as proportions.
The 30-visitor gap may be noise; without a test you cannot separate signal from sampling variation.

steps.prompt: The test gives p = 0.04. The correct conclusion?

options.text: Reject the null at 5%: evidence B differs from A, and the direction favors B
options.why: p < 0.05 with the observed direction favoring B supports a real difference — while reporting the effect size (1.5 percentage points) and CI.

options.text: There is a 96% chance B is better
options.why: A p-value is not the probability the alternative is true — it is P(data this extreme | null).

options.text: p = 0.04 is too close to 0.05 to act on
options.why: The pre-chosen alpha was 0.05; moving the goalpost after seeing the data invalidates the test.

scenarios.title: Formulating an Optimization
scenarios.context: A warehouse must assign delivery routes minimizing total fuel cost. Costs are linear in distance, each truck has a capacity limit, every stop must be visited exactly once. 200 stops, 12 trucks.

steps.prompt: How do you frame this problem?

options.text: Mixed-integer linear program (or VRP heuristic) — discrete routing with capacity constraints
options.why: Visit-once + capacity + linear costs is a vehicle-routing / integer-programming structure; gradient descent cannot handle the discrete assignment.

options.text: Gradient descent on a smooth relaxation of the routes
options.why: Routes are discrete permutations; a smooth relaxation loses the visit-once structure and rounds badly.

options.text: Least squares fit of cost vs distance
options.why: That estimates a cost model — it does not choose routes.

answerBank.q: Prove: the sum of two odd integers is even.
answerBank.a: Write them as 2k+1 and 2m+1. Sum = 2k+2m+2 = 2(k+m+1), which is twice an integer — even by definition. This is a direct proof: unpack the definition, do algebra, repack.

answerBank.q: A fair coin is flipped 100 times; approximate P(heads ≥ 60).
answerBank.a: Binomial(100, 0.5): μ=50, σ=5. CLT: Z=(60−50)/5=2 ⇒ P(Z≥2)≈0.0228 (about 2.3%). With continuity correction, P(X≥59.5): Z=1.9 ≈ 2.9%.

answerBank.q: Why does gradient descent need a small learning rate?
answerBank.a: The update x−α∇f overshoots when α is large relative to the curvature: for convex quadratic with max curvature L, convergence needs α < 2/L. Too large ⇒ oscillation/divergence; too small ⇒ slow but steady.
